title: Stronger economy. Tougher valuation maths.
deck: My read on Wednesday's completed session: the pressure is not simply a weaker-growth story. Stronger activity can support revenues while higher costs and required returns squeeze what investors will pay for them. The useful test is whether durable cash-flow gains can outrun the discount-rate headwind.

sections.title: Higher yields across the curve, not just one maturity.
sections.body: Official Treasury par yields rose to 4.85% at two years, 5.11% at ten years and 5.40% at thirty years on 23 September: daily increases of 14, 15 and 11 basis points. The 10Y–2Y spread moved only from 25 to 26 basis points. My interpretation: the important change was a broadly higher level of yields, not a dramatic change in slope. That raises the hurdle for valuations dependent on distant cash flows. It does not identify how much came from real growth, inflation compensation, policy expectations or term premium; daily observations cannot establish that causal breakdown.

sections.title: Good demand news can still be uncomfortable for shares.
sections.body: S&P Global's September flash composite output index rose to 58.4 from 56.0, while input-cost growth reached a near four-year high. This is a preliminary business survey, not an official GDP or inflation reading. AP's closing figures show the S&P 500 at 7,706.03 (−0.8%), Dow at 51,511.59 (−0.7%) and Nasdaq Composite at 26,936.04 (−1.1%); the Russell 2000 lost 1.8%, all changes rounded. My inference: stronger sales prospects and more expensive capital can pull valuations in opposite directions. The counterargument is genuine operating leverage: businesses able to serve extra demand without proportionate cost increases may still grow cash flows faster. Index declines do not prove that mechanism has failed.

sections.title: Check the oil contract before comparing the headline.
sections.body: AP reported November-delivery Brent at $103.08 per barrel, up 3.9%, while December delivery rose 2.8% to $98.12. Those are different contracts, not contradictory prices for an identical instrument. My assessment: the delivery-month gap makes a generic claim that oil is above or below a round-number threshold less useful than a consistent contract comparison. For a company forecast, exposure depends on purchase timing, hedges and pass-through. S&P Global also noted that competition constrained some selling-price increases. Strong demand therefore need not protect every margin. Sustained lower input costs would weaken this concern; a single cheaper later-dated contract does not settle it.

sections.title: Resilient operations are a counterweight, not a free pass.
sections.body: Cintas reported fiscal first-quarter revenue growth of 10.9%, organic growth of 8.9% and operating margin of 23.6%, versus 22.7% a year earlier, for the period ended 31 August. Its raised annual guidance excludes the proposed UniFirst acquisition's expected impact; adjusted EPS guidance also excludes non-recurring transaction costs. My interpretation: this is company-specific evidence against a blanket collapse in operating performance, not proof of economy-wide resilience or an attractive share price. In the DCF, keep a standalone operating case separate from acquisition scenarios, and test a higher discount rate independently. Do not add hypothetical deal benefits without their funding and integration costs, or substitute adjusted EPS for free cash flow.

watch: Compare final survey readings with subsequent official activity and price data before treating the flash report as confirmed growth or inflation.
Look for repeated evidence of sales growth converting into cash after working capital and investment needs, rather than assuming reported earnings growth is enough.
Track a consistent oil delivery month and company-specific cost pass-through. A sustained reversal in input costs and yields would challenge the valuation-pressure thesis.
caveat: Codex's analysis, not Owen's personal view or investment advice. This brief covers the completed 23 September US session; research concluded on 24 September at the displayed EDT/HKT cutoff, not at the scheduled morning publication time. Treasury values are official daily par-yield observations versus 22 September, not executable quotes. PMI is a preliminary September survey released 23 September. Cintas results were released 23 September but cover the quarter ended 31 August; guidance is forward-looking. Oil figures distinguish November and December delivery. Interpretations and causal explanations are judgments, not established facts.
